A rectangular garden was $50 \mathrm{~m}$ long and $40 \mathrm{~m}$ wide. An artificial lake was built next to it, so that the whole set forms a $60 \mathrm{~m}$ square. Then a fence was stretched, separating both the garden and the lake in two parts with equal areas, as shown in the picture. How long is this fence?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The outer frame in the figure is a square region; the light green rectangular garden is located at the upper left, and the light blue regions on the right side and below form an L-shaped lake. The black lines mark the boundary between the garden and the lake. The red fence is a straight line, entering from the upper side of the square, slanting toward the lower right, passing through the green garden, then passing through the lower blue lake region, and finally reaching the lower side of the square. Reasoning: Let the whole square be 60 m × 60 m, and let the garden be the 50 m × 40 m rectangle in the upper-left corner. Take the upper-left corner of the square as the origin, to the right as x, and downward as y. Let the red fence intersect the upper side at horizontal coordinate a, intersect the lower boundary of the garden y=40 at horizontal coordinate c, and intersect the lower side at horizontal coordinate b. Because the fence is a straight line, c=a+(40/60)(b-a). The fence divides the garden into two parts of equal area. The total area of the garden is 50×40=2000, so the area of the left-side part is 1000. This part is a trapezoid with height 40 and upper and lower parallel sides respectively a and c, so its area is 40(a+c)/2=20(a+c). Thus 20(a+c)=1000, giving a+c=50. The total area of the lake is 60×60−50×40=3600−2000=1600, so each part into which the lake is divided has area 800. The lake region on the left side of the fence is in the bottom strip, and is a trapezoid with height 20 and upper and lower parallel sides respectively c and b, with area 20(c+b)/2=10(c+b). Thus 10(c+b)=800, giving c+b=80. Subtracting a+c=50 from c+b=80 gives b−a=30. The red fence goes from the upper side of the square to the lower side, with vertical direction change 60 m and horizontal direction change 30 m, so its length is sqrt(60^2+30^2)=sqrt(4500)=30sqrt(5) m.

method.method_draft: Coordinate/trapezoid-area route. From the image, model the outer figure as a 60 m by 60 m square, with the 50 m by 40 m garden as the upper-left rectangle and the lake as the remaining L-shaped blue region: a 10 m right strip plus a 20 m bottom strip. Let the red fence meet the top edge of the square/garden at horizontal coordinate a, cross the garden-lake horizontal boundary at y=40 with coordinate c, and meet the bottom edge at coordinate b. Because the fence is a straight line, c=a+(40/60)(b-a). The garden part cut off on the left is a trapezoid of height 40 and parallel sides a and c, and it must have area 1000, half of 50·40, so 20(a+c)=1000, hence a+c=50. The lake part cut off on the left is a trapezoid in the bottom strip of height 20 and parallel sides c and b, and it must have area 800, half of 60^2−50·40, so 10(c+b)=800, hence c+b=80. These equations give b−a=30. Since the red segment runs from top to bottom of the 60 m square, its vertical change is 60 and its horizontal change is 30, so by Pythagoras its length is sqrt(60^2+30^2)=30 sqrt(5) m.

method.method_draft: Center-of-rectangle plus lake-area route. From the image, place coordinates with the 60 m square’s top-left corner as (0,0), x to the right and y downward; the garden is the rectangle 0≤x≤50, 0≤y≤40, and the red fence is a straight line from the top edge to the bottom edge. Since the red line cuts the rectangular garden into two equal areas, use the fact that a straight line bisecting a rectangle in this top-to-bottom fashion passes through the rectangle’s center, (25,20). Let s be the horizontal change of the fence per 1 m vertical drop. Then the fence has x-coordinate 25+20s at the garden-lake boundary y=40 and 25+40s at the bottom y=60. The lake has total area 60^2−50·40=1600, so each lake part has area 800. The left lake piece visible in the bottom strip is a trapezoid of height 20 with parallel horizontal widths 25+20s and 25+40s, so its area is 20·[(25+20s+25+40s)/2]=500+600s. Set 500+600s=800 to get s=1/2. Thus over the full 60 m vertical span, the fence shifts horizontally 60s=30 m, and its length is sqrt(60^2+30^2)=30 sqrt(5) m.

Image description: The diagram shows a large square region. In its upper-left part there is a light green rectangle representing the garden, and the remaining L-shaped blue region represents the lake: a vertical strip on the right and a horizontal strip along the bottom. A red straight fence segment runs from the top edge of the square down to the bottom edge, slanting to the right, and it passes through the garden and then the lake.

Reasoning: Place coordinates with the 60 m square’s top-left corner at (0,0), x to the right and y downward. The garden is the rectangle 0≤x≤50, 0≤y≤40. Since the red fence cuts the rectangular garden into two equal areas and enters/exits the garden through its top and bottom sides, the line must pass through the garden’s center, (25,20).

Let s be the horizontal change of the fence for each 1 m vertical drop. Then the fence has x-coordinate 25+20s at y=40 and x-coordinate 25+40s at y=60.

The total area of the lake is 60^2−50·40=3600−2000=1600, so each half of the lake has area 800.

The left lake part lies in the bottom strip, from y=40 to y=60. Its horizontal widths at the top and bottom are 25+20s and 25+40s, so its area is a trapezoid:
20·[(25+20s+25+40s)/2]=500+600s.
Set this equal to 800:
500+600s=800, so 600s=300 and s=1/2.

Over the full 60 m height, the horizontal shift of the fence is 60·(1/2)=30 m. Therefore the fence length is
sqrt(60^2+30^2)=sqrt(3600+900)=sqrt(4500)=30sqrt(5) m.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The outer frame in the figure is a square region; the light green rectangular garden is located at the upper left, and the light blue regions on the right side and below form an L-shaped lake. The black lines mark the boundary between the garden and the lake. The red fence is a straight line, entering from the upper side of the square, slanting toward the lower right, passing through the green garden, then passing through the lower blue lake region, and finally reaching the lower side of the square.

Reasoning: Let the whole square be 60 m × 60 m, and let the garden be the 50 m × 40 m rectangle in the upper-left corner. Take the upper-left corner of the square as the origin, to the right as x, and downward as y. Let the red fence intersect the upper side at horizontal coordinate a, intersect the lower boundary of the garden y=40 at horizontal coordinate c, and intersect the lower side at horizontal coordinate b. Because the fence is a straight line, c=a+(40/60)(b-a).

The fence divides the garden into two parts of equal area. The total area of the garden is 50×40=2000, so the area of the left-side part is 1000. This part is a trapezoid with height 40 and upper and lower parallel sides respectively a and c, so its area is 40(a+c)/2=20(a+c). Thus 20(a+c)=1000, giving a+c=50.

The total area of the lake is 60×60−50×40=3600−2000=1600, so each part into which the lake is divided has area 800. The lake region on the left side of the fence is in the bottom strip, and is a trapezoid with height 20 and upper and lower parallel sides respectively c and b, with area 20(c+b)/2=10(c+b). Thus 10(c+b)=800, giving c+b=80.

Subtracting a+c=50 from c+b=80 gives b−a=30. The red fence goes from the upper side of the square to the lower side, with vertical direction change 60 m and horizontal direction change 30 m, so its length is sqrt(60^2+30^2)=sqrt(4500)=30sqrt(5) m.
